summary: 149 full occurrences were reviewed; routine_counts is null. Separate repeated tokens in JTM 3.1/26, JTM 5.1/19, MAC NE Unfortunate Youth/8, 69/429 and 94/330 retain individual decisions but are quoted at most once per context.

I uses Preterit Intransitive escape and pursuit; III has an active releasing participant and patient. The Detransitive Part. Pass. mafalte at PrS 80/19 denotes being free, without entailing a preceding release; its existing quotation is retained.

falite/falətto are Part act. in street-roaming; falito is qaṭəl in escape and spirit-loss contexts. PrS 59/25 contrasts Faliti with kfaliti; ko-Preterit is proposed, with dialectal Infectum analysis still a question.
The -lux affected possessor in JTM 3.4/12–13 does not make the survivor an object. The singular falət with distributed plural Christians in JTM 3.2/8,11 is retained as supplied.
ʕal/b-/l-/bayn-/bəṯr- already belong to I.2; b ḥḏoḏe and bayn ḥḏoḏe show reciprocal targets. Abstract bəṯr- pursuit is distinguished from bodily chasing as I.2b.
90/10 contains both an Infectum prohibition and positive Imperativ; the inherited mixed example remains under Imperativ because it contains maflet-a. Its first verb alone is not an Imperativ.
The source at Talay 1/43 verifies the release quotation embedded in the inherited III Infectum note (LB 43); the new standalone quotation does not validate the obsolete 95/210 reference.

New idioms were checked against supplied idioms and permitted lookup searches for maflatle qarʕ, falət ruḥ and ruḥayḏe falito. No additional match was found. Exhalation at 94/392 is retained as literal release of breath, not automatically promoted to an idiom.
The supplied head's Arabic-versus-MEA etymological comment is preserved; this corpus alone cannot adjudicate borrowing.

Jan Beṯ-Şawoce has no edition translation. English quotations below retain the supplied project machine translation and are marked as such; sense decisions rest on the Turoyo. Where available, round-1 proposals are retained in the human layout and counts, and are not resubmitted in this JSON.
Round 1 fills I.1 and I.2 Preterit Intransitive to five and I.2 Infectum to five; readers’ thin-cell counts omit those additions. Routine escape/assault examples are therefore not added again.

falətwo contrasts formally with fəltiwo: the former supports a new Preterit-wa box, while the latter is habitual Infectum-wa. The conditional falət tokens at 1.8/155 are provisionally qaṭəl; conditional meaning does not erase the vowel distinction.
Jan 3.1/18 retains singular-looking falət with plural relative antecedent ar rabe, supporting the agreement variation noted in round 1 without normalisation.
Release after serving a sentence, infant escape from the breast and survival of killing all fit inherited I.1. No new sense or collocation group is explicitly proposed in this input.
94/179 has a partial alignment flag: the German includes details absent from Turoyo. Please verify alignment before publishing any German quotation from this verse; none is quoted here.
At JTM 1.5/19 is the vessel bottom cut out, shaped, or otherwise produced? III.2 deliberately does not choose the operation.
At JTM 2.3/1 are pumpkins left on the plant to mature, or put aside after harvest? Confirm contracted maflətinalle.
At 113/51 and inherited 112/294, does offspring bəṯri mean survival after death, succession, or simply children following the speaker? Verify Infectum fəlto against qaṭəl falito in the edition.
Confirm kfaliti (PrS 59/25) as ko-Preterit, rather than dialectal k-Infectum.
Check consonant order in fətliwa (72/9) and maftlat (90/9); the existing flt spelling differs and ftl is a separate root. No normalized source spelling was introduced.
Is fəlliti (53/149) a productive Part act. or lexical fugitive noun/adjective? The proposed unusual-form example is withheld.
Confirm feminine agreement in falətlux kačke (JTM 3.4/12) and the article/gender of naməs (98/77–78).
PrS 41/65 begins German ie after a split sie; 112/216 lacks the pursuit clause in German. Both are withheld as examples pending source checking.
Does PrS 85/25 Faliti ann əḥrayḏi conventionally mean urgent defecation or an actual accident? The German euphemism alone cannot establish an idiom.
112/371 names Baschto as seeing in German, while the Turoyo ḥzele l Bašto may reverse seer and target. Preserve the edition wording but check participant alignment before editorial approval.
57/89 mafəltile may be a contracted Preterit or plural Infectum; retain the reader's Infectum provisionally and verify the paradigm.
At 1.8/155 confirm falət in both ənkan clauses: qaṭəl in an open condition, or a Jan vowel variant of Infectum folət? No form example depends on this provisional correction.
At 3.1/18 confirm singular-looking falət with plural ar rabe; compare round-1 collective agreement observations.
Correct engleiten → entgleiten in sense 1
rationale: The German infinitive meaning slip away is entgleiten. Engleiten is a missing-t typo in this synonym list.

summary: Correct als dass Wort → als das Wort
rationale: Wort requires the neuter article das, not the conjunction dass. The supplied edition translation likewise reads Als das Wort.

summary: Restore r in hinterliesse
rationale: The German verb is hinterlassen; hinteliesse is missing the r of hinter-. Preserve the entry's existing ss spelling.

summary: Inanimate subject types include a club slipping from a hand (PrS 33/41), a gun going off (PrS 39/24), bodily waste escaping (PrS 85/25), and breath/spirit escaping (112/226); word escaping a mouth is already in the entry.
The same pursuit/assault frame admits animals, ants, a personified wind, food, and reciprocal sexual revelry. These contexts do not independently justify new lexical senses.
Inanimate releasing subjects include frost and a moistened material; inanimate patients include a chain, game pieces and breath. Physical release remains unchanged.

summary: Bee-swarm emergence is an animate collective extension of free emergence/escape, not a new swarming sense.
ʕal-target with bax xabre and baṣ ṣuʕre denotes verbal assault, preserving the hostile attack frame rather than creating a separate speaking sense.
mede m iḏayye lə kfolət extends slipping from a hand to retaining control. The inherited falito m-i=iḏo idiom already supplies the lost-control/opportunity metaphor; no duplicate idiom is proposed.
